MR. THOMPSON (RED DEER)-ALLEGED MISSTATEMENT BY MINISTER ABOUT REPRESENTATIONS ON ESTATE TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege relating to remarks that were made last night during the "late show" by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). These remarks were in reply to a complaint that was legitimately made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in regard to a press release that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on January 28 and provided to this newspaper by the hon. members for Portage (Mr. Cobbe) and Provencher (Mr. Smerchanski). Their release dealt with changes in the estates tax that they said would be brought about by the finance ministry.
As a result of the complaint made by the hon. member for Edmonton West in regard to members of the government party making statements to the press in advance of a policy statement being made to the house about government policy, the Minister of Finance stated, as reported in Hansard at page 5160:
First of all, in respect to the estate tax I did not receive a single letter or request for a meeting from any member of the opposition. Secondly, I should like to say that the most frequent submissions with regard to the estate tax dealt with the level of the exemptions and difficulties concerning payment of estate tax, as well as with what would happen to the estates of people who died before the law came into effect. Everybody knew this except the opposition members, who were not paying any attention to what was happening.
I rise on this point of privilege because I believe that the Minister of Finance is either ignorant of what comes into his office, is not aware of what is being said in the House of Commons, or else is intentionally misrepresenting the facts. I say this because this statement is not according to the facts.
A little further on in the debate I myself pointed out that I had received more than
1,000	letters protesting against the estate tax, in reply to which the minister said:
Why did the hon. member not speak to me about the matter or send me the letters?
I would remind the minister that I did write him a letter, to which was attached a number of petitions; I did not bother him with the individual letters. The text of the letter is as follows:
I am enclosing herewith copies of several petitions which have been received from communities in my constituency protesting against the pending estate tax which, together with the flood of mail to this date, reaches well into the hundreds. It is my impression that public opinion is overwhelmingly against this bill. I believe that such legislation, if enacted, can prove extremely detrimental whether it affects farm, business or home. It will also, in my opinion, be harmful to the economy in the sense that it will discourage initiative and, at the same time, drive much needed capital out of the country. I believe that you would be well advised to modify or withdraw altogether this part of the current budget proposal.
I have not received, as yet, a reply to this letter.
I wrote a similar letter to the Prime Minister, who did have the courtesy to reply. On January 30 I received the following letter from the Office of the Prime Minister:
On behalf of the Prime Minister, I acknowledge with thanks receipt of your letter of January 29, enclosing copies of several petitions from communities in your constituency, protesting against the pending estate tax.
Your comments regarding public reaction to this bill are being brought to Mr. Trudeau's attention.
I am not the only one in the opposition to protest against the new estate tax. Many others in the opposition protested. I know the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), spoke directly to the minister about this.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORTED INCREASE IN RADIATION LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, National
Health and Welfare officials have confirmed that radioactivity detected in air filter samples from Fort William, Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal increased between December 11 and December 15. No danger to public health was involved. Because of the small samples involved, it was impossible to determine whether, in fact, this increase could be attributed directly to the United States Schooner explosion test, which took place in Nevada on December 8. However, the coincidence with correspondingly higher levels reported in the United States some days earlier was brought to the attention of United States authorities.
No comment has been offered formally, but liaison concerning the levels of radioactivity is continuing. Because the higher readings could not be attributed directly to the schooner test, no formal representations were made to the United States authorities.
I should also point out that this test explosion was intended to explore possible peaceful applications for nuclear explosions in which Canada has been interested. The Canadian authorities were informed in advance of all details regarding the proposed test.

During the three month period since reform of the estate and gift taxes was announced in the budget, the country has engaged in a lively debate about the government's proposals. Some of the argument has been misleading and destructive, such as the expensive advertising claiming that the legislation means the end of family farms and small businesses, or that the whole thing is a communist conspiracy. This is just not the case. But there have been many constructive arguments. With some exceptions, Members of Parliament have tried to sift fact from fiction. They have tried to influence the government to legislate in the best interests of their constituents. This constructive attitude means, I believe, that most members and most Canadians recognize that the proposals represent a reform. They recognize that while we are retaining the estate tax, we should change the structure of exemptions to help widows, widowers and young children.
At the start of this discussion on second reading I want to describe to hon. members some of my reactions to the public debate. My mail and the discussion inside and outside parliament convince me that the criticism is far out of proportion to the impact of estate taxes. Ninety-five per cent of Canadians never pay any estate taxes at all, and we expect this ratio to stay about the same in the future. As for those 5 per cent who will pay some tax, more than half of the revenues are collected from estates valued at $500,000 or more. I can only conclude that much of the confusion and criticism results from misrepresentation of the government's proposal, though not all, of course. Some individuals have looked at the tables and concluded correctly that certain estates will pay more tax. For others, the October announcement may have been an emotional shock which forced them to think about their estate situations for the first time in their lives. Some mail I have received indicates clearly that a number of the writers thought there was no estate tax in Canada before last October.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
My second reaction is that a good deal of the opposition stems from the view held by some persons that there should be no estate tax at all. These persons and groups condemn the proposed reform, but few suggest a return to the old system. They seem to want to have their cake and eat it too. They are not the government and they do not have to raise
DEBATES	5179
Income Tax Act and Estate Tax Act the funds to pay for the expenses of the state in creating an economic climate in which business can survive. Therefore they are seemingly unworried about the revenues that would be lost through abolition of the estate tax.
More than $200 million a year is raised through the estate tax and provincial succession duties. Some critics might argue that we could do away with this kind of tax if governments tightened their belts and reduced spending by this amount. Our conclusion as a government is that the estate tax is a fair and equitable part of our total tax system regardless of the amount of revenues we need.
This is because governments have at their disposal only two forms of taxation which are progressive. By "progressive" I mean a tax which can be weighted to take relatively more money from the wealthier persons in our society and relatively less from the poor. The two progressive taxes are the income tax and the estate tax. The rising demand for services from all levels of government makes it unlikely that the total revenues of government can be reduced. Therefore those who would abolish the estate tax and gift tax must produce a satisfactory alternative to raise more than $200 million for governments at the two levels.
We estimate that to raise about this amount from roughly the same group of persons who pay the bulk of estate taxes, that is, those with incomes over $10,000, would require a 15 per cent income surtax. If, instead, we raised this amount in income taxes from those whose estates are over $500,000 we would have to double their present income tax. Before proposing an end to estate taxes, abolitionists should produce a convincing argument that increases in income taxes of this dimension will not adversely affect incentive, will not speed up our brain drain and curb our rate of capital investment.
Perhaps the abolitionists would prefer that the same revenues be raised from all income groups instead of from those who pay most of our estate taxes now. At present fewer than 5 per cent of the population pays any estate tax. To spread the cost of this revenue loss to all taxpayers would, for instance, require an estimated increase of almost 1 per cent in the social development tax.

speechtext:
I do not have this information in front of me though 1 have seen it. I will be pleased to give it to my hon. friend before this debate is over. But I should point out that the changes in estate tax are not designed to take more money out of the Canadian economy. What they are designed to do is to help widows, young orphaned families and disabled children, and other people will have to pay for this. So there is a shift in the burden.
There are other reasons why an estate tax is desirable. Nowadays it is an integral part of the taxation system of most western countries. Our two major trading partners, the United States and Britain, raise a larger portion of their total government revenues from inheritance taxes than does Canada. Despite the opposition of a vocal minority through the years, the majority in all these countries consider it a fair tax.
In Canada, where about seven million persons pay income tax, it is fair that the relatively few who have accumulated the greatest wealth should contribute at death to the common good of our country. They are usually the ones who have benefited most from the collective effort of Canadians to build a strong economic and political system.
Federal abdication from the estate tax field probably would not result in their abolition in all ten provinces. Royal commissions in Ontario and Quebec, where two-thirds of our population resides, have recommended their continuation in one form or another. The provinces now receive about three-quarters of the money we collect through estate taxes. One should consider the provincial revenue requirements at this time before engaging in any wishful thinking about the total abolition of death taxes in Canada.


There has been a good deal of discussion recently in the prairie provinces about inheritance taxes. One province has abolished them, another is committed to doing so and a third is apparently considering such a change. Following their weekend meeting, the premiers of the three provinces sent a telegram asking us to postpone legislative consideration of this bill pending consultations with the provinces.
I would like to place on the record my reaction to these various developments. In provinces where the tax is refunded any changes in the federal law will not affect provincial revenues. A federal-provincial conference has been held since the reform was announced last October and there has been a good deal of criticism of our putting off introduction of the bill from October till the present time. At that federal-provincial conference I indicated that interested provinces would have every opportunity they desired to raise the subject with me. There was also consultation concerning the estate tax following publication of the Carter royal commission report on taxation.
I believe that this government has always made it clear to the provinces that any changes must first be proposed to parliament. In taxation matters in Canada we cannot go to the provinces and say that we are going to make these changes before we tell the parliament of Canada. Our responsibility is first of all to the members of this house. To do otherwise in our system of responsible government would, I believe, be improper.
Once the government decided to retain the estate tax it had to decide whether the tax was being levied in the fairest possible way. It considered, but rejected, the recommendations of the Carter royal commission on taxation which would have doubled the revenue from taxation of inheritances.

speechtext: Why?

Why? Because we decided that a buck is not a buck is not a buck. Instead it decided to keep the revenue yield about the same while instituting reforms to help widows, widowers and young children in this country.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
On this point I was interested to read a report yesterday, I believe, which said that the United States treasury department has proposed that in the United States action be taken similar to ours to allow tax free transfers between spouses in that country. The
February 5, 1969	COMMONS
reform to exempt from taxation transfers between spouses is most significant for widows. It recognizes the contribution wives make to the accummulation of a family's wealth, but it also does much more. It helps to take care of a social need. On average, wives outlive husbands by at least seven years. If the husbands are Members of Parliament the wives probably outlive them by 10 years or even 20 years. In half the cases where estate taxes are collected there is a surviving widow. Most of us know of families where the father has died and the children have had to leave school early because there is a lack of money in the family. The reform removes any influence the estate tax may have had in these unfortunate situations. Annuities left to widows will now bear no federal estate tax. We expect this change to take on increasing importance in future years because of the tremendous growth in pension plans as well as the increasing benefits that will accrue under that excellent piece of legislation, the Canada Pension Plan.
Besides the basic $20,000 exemption for all estates valued at more than $50,000, a new exemption of $10,000 is provided for all adult children, that is, for children 26 years of age and over. For all healthy children receiving bequests of $10,000 or more there is an extra $1,000 exemption for each year the child is less than 26 years of age. This means that a healthy child under one year of age might receive an exemption of $35,000. For an incapacitated child, that is, a child which is unable to support itself, the total exemption may be as much as $80,000.
May I give some examples of how the new exemptions will work. First of all, certain estates left to widows are exempt. If a husband died-he would be a father-and had four children whose ages were 18, 16, 14 and 7 years, he could leave $105,000 on which no estate tax would be levied. He could leave that on top of any amount he might leave to his widow.
I think there is no quarrel about helping widows and small children. A good deal of the criticism about the reform, indeed, about retaining estate taxes at all, centres upon its effects on family businesses and family farms. Some groups have suggested total or partial exemptions for these kinds of enterprises. We believe this is not reasonable and I wish to explain our thinking at some length at this time.
During his lifetime the farmer or the small businessman benefits from government programs and from the general well-being of the 29180-328

Once exceptions are made for one group in society other groups feel aggrieved and demand the same privilege. Special privileges can also cause distortions in the effects of a tax system. Exempting farms, for instance, would encourage land buying by wealthy non-farmers seeking to avoid the payment of estate taxes. A development of this kind would only add to our difficulties with land speculation in the country and especially around our major urban areas.
An estate tax may place a special burden on estates in which the major assets are not liquid. I admit that. But how great is the burden? Let us consider a case where the impact is most severe, where a father leaves an estate directly to one son without any use of the $2,000 annual gifting provision prior to death. In that case the father would not have availed himself of provisions allowing him to sell the farm or the business to his son, something many fathers do when they contemplate passing their property on to a son. In the worst case, and we are considering a $200,000 estate-that is a net estate; after provision for all liabilities have been made the estate would be worth $200,000 in cash-the tax would be $43,200, or slightly less than 22 per cent of the value of the business. This falls well within the bounds of liabilities assumed by many Canadians as a matter of course. I do not think anyone would acquire a $200,000 business without assuming a liability against it of at least $43,000. By way of contrast, when a business is purchased, or if a farm is sold, it is normal for the incoming or new entrepreneur to assume a liability against that business or farm totalling 75 per cent of its worth, as against the 22 per cent tax liability that must be assumed by those inheriting businesses or farms under the worst conditions where the inheritance is worth $200,000 net.

As a result of the new estate tax rates people will be tempted to say to themselves: Once I have got it made I will get out.
Estates in Canada of $250,000 or even of $100,000 are not usually inherited wealth, certainly not in the provinces where a great deal of development has taken place. In the last 20 years many men in the province of Alberta who started out with a mortgaged property on which there was a large lien are today worth $250,000 or $500,000 simply because they had the guts, energy and initiative to work hard and become successful. Now we are going to penalize these people. This legislation is the greatest killer of initiative to be found. I speak as one who comes from that area of the country and I am sure the same holds true in many parts of Canada.
Yet the minister cites to us examples in Great Britain and the United States, both countries which have accumulative wealth. People in Great Britain exported their capital to the United States when the United States was in process of development. The United States is now exporting capital to Canada. We need capital. Yet when we ask Canadians to save, to invest in Canadian enterprise, when we tell them, "Don't spend, put your money to work," at the same time we tell them, "We will tax you because the more you save the more you have, and so the more we will take away from you."
I find this an extraordinary philosophy. On previous occasions when major changes in estate taxes have been proposed it has been customary to provide for some breathing space between the public announcement of the new policy and the actual implementation. Eor example, the present Estate Tax Act was first introduced, if I recall correctly, in late 1957 or early 1958. The bill was given first reading but was not proceeded with in order

to give the public an opportunity to make representations concerning hardships and anomalies contained in the draft legislation. May I say that the estate tax principle was far ahead of the succession duty principle. Yet by these proposals we are abandoning the estate tax principle and going back to the succession duty principle in part. To me this is a regressive step.
The present act was reintroduced in parliament in the fall of 1958 and was passed on September 6, 1958. However, and this is a significant point, it was not proclaimed in force until January 1, 1959 in order to give both the professional advisers and the persons affected an opportunity to examine their situation and to make the necessary changes. It was applicable only to estates of persons who died on or after January 1, 1959. Thus, not only was the public made aware of the proposed changes and given an opportunity to seek improvements in the legislation but when the legislation was actually passed a further period was granted to enable persons to rearrange their wills and financial affairs to fit the new legislation.
There is no doubt that the present proposals contain radical changes in the Estate Tax Act, and the effective date of the proposals has been stated to be October 22 last. The minister made an announcement on January 31 and people were prejudiced as a result of the government not announcing for over three months an optional date for the coming into effect of the present proposals. I do not think it is fair to approach the matter in this way.
I remember the two-month period after the budget disclosures and prior to the minister's press release on December 27 when all sorts of things were bothering tax advisers. First of all, they could not tell anybody if they could include a common disaster provision in a will. This applies whether the will covers a $5,000, $20,000 or $100,000 estate. I suppose I should not use the figure $5,000 and instead say $25,000 because at that time the exemption was only $20,000. But it was unclear at that time whether these wills could include a common disaster clause. The minister cleared up this matter, but that was two months after the disclosure of the proposals.
Then there were questions concerning exoneration clauses and remarriage clauses which appear in, shall we say, 80 per cent of wills other than simple wills. Yet there was this delay. It is no wonder so many letters were received protesting the uncertainty that

this created. I do not know whether it was a design of this participatory government that this be done merely to excite the populace, create uncertainty and get them to debate estate taxation, but certainly the effect was very profound.

While this tone might be expected in a post-revglutionary emerging state, it is both unbecoming and saddening to see it urged upon a young country competing for world markets, seeking talented people, and constantly requiring risk capital, all to the purpose of sponsoring a dynamic and productive wealth-base."

The government claimed in its budget speech that it was not accepting the Carter concept. But it now appears to have out-Cartered Carter.
As of Oct. 22, gifts will be taxed, not at rates stopping at 28 per cent, but escalating to 75 per cent. Clearly the making of large gifts will stop.
And the $40,000 estate tax exemption is cut to $20,000, while the tax rates are steeply escalated so that the privilege of paying 50 per cent of one's life savings is achieved once one's estate reaches $300,000.
What is the purpose of these tax changes? Is it to accomplish an increase in government revenues? In the light of the budgetary problems facing the government one would have thought the budgetary proposals would be designed to provide more revenue for the government, but instead we have legislation through these estate tax proposals which is asocial. Yet this legislation, because it is introduced through a budget proposal, does not go to a standing committee and is not subject to comment by the public through representations. Other legislation, such as a broadcasting bill, a bill on drug prices or something else, would of course go to a standing committee and the people would have a chance to comment on it. But no, not in this case. Simply by raising the gift tax to a high of 75 per cent and imposing estate tax rates based on what a man has at his death plus

Since we have operated until now on a system in which private property rights are important, it is only right that any negation of those rights should not be achieved through tax law. I think these comments by Mr. Asper are legitimate. I do not intend to go into the details of the schedules and so on because we can take any kind of situation. We can find examples under certain circumstances where at a particular time it would appear that the tax payable today on the assumption of death in the future, assuming the values to be today's values and not the values at the time of death, is less under these proposals than under the present estate tax. But equally-and I have any number of examples-it would appear that the tax incidence will be much higher and much more punitive.
If hon. members will bear with me I might go through a typical example in business. The minister discussed the situation of a farmer with one child. He indicated how much tax would be levied on an estate with a net value of $200,000 in the case of a farm and indicated that there would be some $40,000 payable in estate tax and that this was a fair proposition for one son to take on. Of course that does not take into consideration how much the son may have worked on the farm. He may have worked for practically nothing for many years contributing to the farm and this is his reward.
Let us look at another example. Certainly in my part of the world and I am sure in the part of the world of many hon. members it is a typical example. Say that a father when he starts out saves his money. He has a job, saves his money and at age 35 is able to buy or found a company with a capital of $200,000. Assume that he had $50,000 himself and financed the remainder. This typical business could earn $40,000 per year before tax.
This man has two sons who have worked with him over the years. He himself draws a salary of $10,000 a year, pays tax on that salary and puts the remaining $30,000 in the company which is taxed in the amount of $17,000 per year. This leaves an income after tax for the company of $23,000. From this amount the father extracts a dividend of $13,000 on which even after dividend tax credits he is taxed. He leaves $10,000 in the business for expansion and uses his dividend

He leaves $100,000 to his wife with which to buy an annuity, and the two sons inherit the business. It is now earning $150,000 a year before taxes. At present rates this would mean about $80,000 after taxes. Based on the estate tax valuation method used at the present time the business is valued at $800,000. Under the new estate tax the tax would be $340,000 on $800,000, 42 per cent of what is inherited. These sons are 45 and 50 years of age. Yes, but under the present tax all the gifts he gave during his lifetime are brought into his estate, so whether the shares were given before or after death matters little because they are all brought into the same basket and the sons are no farther ahead.
In any event, the only way the sons can keep the business is by borrowing $400,000. They could then pay about $60,000 in income tax and the remaining $340,000 would cover estate taxes. It would not be the company borrowing the money to pay the tax but the sons borrowing the money so that as the new owners with personal responsibility they could pay the tax. Therefore the company which at the time of death was worth $800,000 clear would now find itself owing $400,000. All the sons would see ahead of them would be the prospect of spending the rest of their working lives taking low wages and


paying 63 per cent in income tax and the rest of the earnings to pay back the $400,000 and at least another $400,000 in interest charges on the loan. Why should these boys not sell to foreign interests?
Let no one suggest that this is not being done. I know from personal experience how and why this is being done. It is being done because of the way Canadian tax law is being applied. Growing businesses are being sold to foreign interests. The heirs are quite prepared to take the capital gain they have earned. They take the $800,000, the proceeds of the sale, pay the $340,000 in estate tax and invest $460,000 in C.M.H.C. mortgages which pay 9.3 per cent interest. They then live comfortably on the income and never work another day in their lives. This is a typical example and I repeat, this is what is happening. Men in their forties who have worked day and night almost like demons for seven days a week to put together a viable business, because of the incidence of tax take the first good offer of a sale to foreign interests and then retire. What a shameful loss this is to this country. These people ask themselves the question, why should they be faced with this situation? They obviously decide to get out.
My criticism of the estate tax proposal is not that its greatest impact is on the very wealthy, and I made that clear at the beginning. What is the nature of estates in Canada? I am informed that in 1966, of about $900 million in taxable value of estates only 72 had assets of more than $1 million and that this total reflected 15 per cent. I suggest it is the small and middle-size estates that will be hit. In 1966, of 5,700 taxable estates, 4,694 or 82 per cent had taxable assets ranging from $50,000 to $300,000 and of these about 70 per cent were less than $100,000. Previously these estates were untaxed. They will now be subject to tax, although the number has been diminished tremendously by the changes proposed by the minister on January 30. These middle-range estates will feel the new rates the hardest.
We should not be concerned about any particular group of taxpayers caught by the provisions of this act. Our legitimate concern should be for all taxpayers. By far, however, the impact is much greater in respect of the broad strata of Canadians whose estates will exceed a net of $50,000 and reach up over $300,000. These are estates of independent businessmen, farmers and professionals, the broad middle class of this country. They are the ones to be hit by the estate tax and they also pay the heaviest income tax.

We must remember that estates are accumulated with tax paid dollars. These are the people for whom the minister has always expressed solicitous concern. We now see that this concern is a sham. I could quote from representations made by the construction association. In this field we find small contractors and large construction companies. Many of them are family concerns which will be adversely affected by these tax proposals.
I do not intend to go into detail about the changes proposed by the minister on January 30, but I should like to point out that on page 2 of the communique the minister refers to the $50,000 starting point and indicates in the third paragraph that this will mean, for example, that a small estate left by a brother to a sister or a grandfather to his grandchildren will not be subject to estate tax. In other words, if the estate is less than $50,000 the range of gifts is limitless. However, if the estate happens to be over $50,000 then one must look out because gifts other than those to a spouse will be subject to heavy tax.
Let me now refer to the question of instalment payments. We have been hoping to see this for quite some time. This is not the result of new representations. My colleague, the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales), has had resolutions on the order paper for years in respect of instalment payments on estate taxes to avoid fire sales. The fact that there have been options open to the minister in cases of hardship does not alter the situation. The difficulties involved have been so great it was almost impossible for any estate to qualify, and there were very few which did qualify for deferment. I wonder how many companies were sold literally on a fire-sale basis and bought cheaply by foreign interests or larger Canadian entities? These fire-sales have taken place because the heirs to the estates had to pay estate taxes but had no liquid assets. If the minister would like to know what the effect is on estates which cannot be liquidated easily he should consider large farms such as those which exist in western Canada, or perhaps large companies existing in eastern Canada which are privately owned or closely held.

Mr. Speaker, like most members of this house I have received an inordinately large number of letters on the subject of estate taxes. Not since Nosey Charlie appeared on the balcony have I received as much correspondence, some of which was perhaps no more relevant than the statement made by the aforementioned gentleman.
I come to this debate with a considerable amount of anger over what 5 per cent of our population is doing to the 95 per cent who do not have estates to worry about. I marvel at the fact that these people can make use of advertisements to frighten almost the entire population into believing that everything they have worked for or owned is going to be confiscated. This is a typical example of what has gone on in our society since the beginning of its history. The very rich who do not wish to pay taxes try to convince those who will not be paying them that their interests are alike, in other, words, that the rich man is really and sincerely concerned about the poor man. The unfortunate thing about the situation is that so often these people are successful in their campaigns.
We have only to look through the newspapers to see what is being done. One would have thought from the advertisements and articles that have been appearing that every house and every car were going to be taken away. There has been no balance and no perspective in this whole debate. I took the occasion to make a personal call in reply to most of the letters that came to me because I knew some of the people who had written them. I could not understand their concern because I knew they did not have an estate that large, so what were they worried about? Some of them believed what they had read. Some of them had listened to one radio commentator who told them that 75 per cent of everything they had would be taken away. They also believed the stories that appeared in some of the farm journals and magazines that they would be deprived of the fruits of their work. When it was explained to them that the bill contains practically no change from the present law they were surprised.


I resent the people who spread this propaganda. They are full of cynicism in not standing up and making an argument giving the reasons why they should not be taxed. There is cynicism in trying to persuade and to make propaganda to convince those whose interests are not the same as theirs that they are in the same boat. I am angry at the Tweedledee and Tweedledum debate that has preceded this bill. One would think that the government has brought in some magnificent reform. What has it really done? Let us give it credit for some things that it has done. It has made it possible and universal that wives will not have to pay tax. This is a good thing, but is it really so new? After all, most estate planners made that provision for wives in the past. The government has made the tax somewhat more progressive at some levels but it has not altered the whole package. It has not increased the proportion of our revenues from this particular source but merely shuffled it around.
We are not asking who is more progressive in this debate as between the government and its nemesis in the opposition but who is most reactionary, because it is very hard to say on which side in this debate a reformer should stand. When I listen to spokesmen for the government I become incensed at what they are trying to palm off on the Canadian people as a worth-while reform. It is no such thing. It has made no major concession to the principle of equity. Then I have to listen to what is said by members of the Official Opposition, to the irrational arguments they have dragged out of the nineteenth century.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) pointed out that had he acted on the basis of the Carter recommendations the revenue obtained from estate taxation would have been doubled. That is the position he should have taken instead of the kind of proposal we are considering now. I know thousands of people who are not sure how they will be able to meet their rent obligation. They are taxed on every single thing they buy. I find it difficult to work up sympathy for the poor, unfortunate child who only has half a million dollars left after tax. At least a quarter of the population of this country is living in poverty. These people do not even know whether they can secure accommodation for themselves or their children and their prospects are not very bright. If tears are to be shed in this chamber, let us shed them for those who deserve them.
When the Minister of Finance introduced his budget I had the opportunity to present my views on his proposals. I said then I thought it was a very reactionary and regressive budget. All of us, to some extent, take positions which arise from our experience and background. I have to admit that this is true in my case and that to some extent this debate has, for me, a personal aspect. It is also the case that my party has very strong feelings on this matter. We are a party that believes in equal treatment and fairness in the tax system, that each member of our society should be willing to carry his share of the challenges and responsibilities of that society.
Earlier I said that poverty in Canada has been carefully and incontrovertibly documented. We are not going to cure poverty by talking about it but by raising sufficient revenue to cope with it. What is necessary is a just and fair distribution of the resources of our society. We must have some sense of priority, of what is important and what is not important. I suggest to hon. members that the urgent need of society today is to find revenue to meet the needs of those people who are living at a level at which no human being should be asked to exist. These poor people are not to be blamed any more than the rich man is to be congratulated. I recall a famous cartoon that appeared during a United States presidential election campaign which depicted one of the candidates looking accusingly at a beggar and saying: "Well, it's your own damn fault for not having been born to a father who owns a department store." We may laugh at that sort of thing but we do tend to make this kind of value judgment.
It is not enough that the poor of our society inherit the disadvantages of their condition, that in so many cases these people are born with ill health or born into an unnecessarily harsh and unfeeling environment. On top of all this they suffer the disadvantage of having their needs ignored.
On the other hand, if the sons of rich men were never left any money they would be infinitely better off than the poor people I am talking about. First of all, they would be better cared for because their parents were in a


position to care for them and had the money to do so. How much more advantage do we give to those who have already been born into advantage?
I have heard on many occasions about the terrible things that will happen to the poor if they are given welfare or are helped. They will, I think the phrase is, lose their backbone. It seems to be a terrible thing to give somebody welfare or something which he has not earned by working. What about welfare for the rich? It does not seem to affect their backbone at all. No one seems to worry that an inheritance of $500,000 will affect the beneficiary's backbone. These people must have a different kind of anatomy from the poor, and the chances are they will probably do less well with it.
Another assumption that is made, one which I heard argued in this house a short while ago, is that it almost seems as though the wealth that an individual accumulates is entirely due to his own efforts. No thought or consideration is given to the inputs of our social system. Where would the rich be unless they could move their goods to market, unless there were forces to protect them against fire and disasters of various kinds, unless people were trained and educated to operate their enterprises? People of initiative, people who work hard and build up businesses, are entitled to credit. But so is society, and let us not forget that. No man can build anything on his own. He does it with the assistance of his wife, the people who work for him and all those around him in this nation. Therefore we have to assume that he has some sense of obligation, of responsibility to those who have helped him and made his success possible. Is this so much to ask? Is this such a terrible thing?
Historically speaking, if we removed the words "estate tax" from this debate and substituted "corporation tax" or "income tax", we would find that the arguments were just the same. I was reading a debate which took place in 1917, I believe, when income tax was first introduced in this country. At that time the tax was very small but it was going to change our whole social system. Business was going to collapse, it was said. The world was coming to an end. The pools of private capital needed to develop this country were going to disappear.
Although it may be anarchy, is it so terrible to yell "communism" any more? After all, the Minister of Finance has been accused of being a communist in almost every journal in

this country, so I guess that makes it legitimate now. We have heard this argument before and it has been a bad argument. One would think that General Motors was run like a corner grocery store. Today most of the financing and capital accumulation in our society does not depend upon private pools of wealth. We are only kidding ourselves if we argue that we can advance this country by means of small private pools of wealth and therefore, so it is argued, can reduce taxation and people can keep everything they earn. It is just not that kind of world.
We in this party feel very strongly for people like small businessmen and farmers, who in some ways are in a special position in our society. The small businessman and the farmer are more than just economic units. I have never been a farmer but I have been a small businessman and I know that many small businessmen might be better off working for somebody else if they were to calculate the number of hours they put in. I speak now as one who has put in long hours, and perhaps even made some mistakes, and I can tell the house that I could have worked for somebody else and made more. However, it was my decision to make. Nobody told me to open up a business. Nobody came to me on their knees pleading with me to go into business. I went into business because I chose to do so and because I wanted that kind of life. But I have asked as a small businessman for what I think farmers are also entitled to ask, namely, that if my business has to be sold but my family, my children in particular, wish to preserve it, then an opportunity should be provided for continuance of the enterprise. This is the case in this legislation, as it has been the case in previous legislation. This legislation spells it out a little more specifically, and to that extent we have been given an advantage.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not planned to speak on this bill. I thought that the quicker it was passed the sooner it might be some help to the farmers,
February 5, 1969

Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act but after hearing the Minister without Portfolio last night I think I should try to set the record straight. He misrepresented the situation to members of his own party who are not familiar with western Canada when he said, as recorded on page 5148 of Hansard:
Again, members of the opposition have used the three-bushel quota in an attempt to assess blame in connection with that. I should like to draw their attention to the many months which went by after that quota had been brought into effect before they began to think they could use it for petty political advantage, though they welcomed it at the beginning.
I think this is a terrible statement to be made by one who should be familiar with the situation. The government put a three-bushel quota on damp grain, but what good did it do? It was detrimental to western farmers because in many cases they would have been better off to leave their wheat lying in the swath inasmuch as they found out later that there was no room in the elevators for the damp grain. Farmers in my own constituency had only a one-bushel quota and they were not able to take advantage of the three-bushel quota. The three-bushel damp grain quota was useless in my constituency.
Just yesterday I was in contact with the largest shipping area in my constituency and I was informed it still has only a one-bushel quota and, as one man put it to me, it has not had a box car since God knows when. If this is all the minister saw of the seriousness of the situation when he was out west I think he had better go back there again and take another look.
The situation is very critical. Yesterday I was informed that very little, if any, drying equipment has been placed in position in the Meadow Lake area. It is being moved into position, but I point out that we are now in the month of February. Why was this equipment not put into position much earlier? The minister talked about drying charges of eight cents to ten cents a bushel, but the reports I received from my constituency say the charges run from 18 cents to 20 cents a bushel.
Furthermore, in this difficult situation for western farmers I understand that few, if any, payments have been made under P.F.A.A. This is something this glorified parliamentary secretary should start looking into. I have not yet heard of one single P.F.A.A. payment going out to my constituency although many districts there have had crop failures.

On September 25 last year I asked the Minister of Agriculture to inquire whether a survey of P.F.A.A. needs was being made. We are now well into the month of February and I have not heard that one single farmer in my constituency has received a payment under P.F.A.A. I thought this was a matter which I should bring to the attention of the house.
I certainly welcome any assistance that this legislation will provide farmers to meet the cost of drying their grain. As I say, the three-bushel damp grain quota encouraged many farmers to thresh damp grain when it would have been better to leave it lying in the swath until good weather in the spring. As I indicated at the outset of my remarks, I thought the record should be put straight about the very serious situation in western Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last night I was surprised at the partisan way in which the Minister without Portfolio spoke. I am interested in this legislation and in the support it has received from the opposition, but now the government is trying to take considerable credit for this important step.
I have been long enough in this house to see the farming situation in western Canada deteriorate on at least four occasions and the situation that has developed this year occurred on each of those four occasions. By August last it was realized by western farmers, members of the government and members of the opposition that a serious situation was developing. By September, when grain was in the harvesting stage, people were able to ascertain that there would be a great problem to meet in drying damp grain. But when members of the opposition brought this matter to the attention of the government, what did the government do? Frankly, I am not sure what it did but I am sure of what it did not do. It did not really get around to solving the problem.
When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce returns from the west I am quite sure the recommendation he will make will be to appoint a controller to regulate the flow of grain. It is all very well to supply a farmer in a desperate position with an additional $600, which in effect will be a debt, and ask him to dry wheat, but is it not time we got around to handling the wheat we have on a more equitable basis? Every day some hon. member gets up and asks why we are not able to fill the ships waiting at the ports on the west coast. Then the question is asked what assistance is being given to those areas
February 5, 1969	COMMONS
where damp grain is such a serious problem, and why an open quota is not put on damp grain so that it can be dried. The situation is now so bad that the damp grain will not even be any use for commercial feed come springtime.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I notice in the Western Producer that in some areas the unit quota has not been fulfilled, and on the prairies there are 345 points where the unit quota is not available. At the other end of the picture you will find there are some areas which have a four bushel quota. There are 329 prairie shipping points which are on a three-bushel quota today. Obviously there is inequality in this regard.
The minister made an attack on hon. members. I have heard this sort of thing many times not only from this government but from the previous government. On every occasion when the problem finally was settled it was because the government appointed an overall controller to deal with it. A controller would decide where the grain would be moved from, from what farm points, from what country elevators, and he would decide what box cars would be delivered to the elevators and what grain would be moved from the inland terminals to the coastal terminals. He would also have control over the vessels and the expenses that were incurred by the vessels.
Let us make no mistake about this. It does not do any good for farmers to pay the demurrage in respect of boats which cannot be filled through no responsibility of theirs but through the inability of the transportation facilities, the Canadian Wheat Board and the Board of Grain Commissioners to put the proper grade of grain in position for loading. If this advance of $600 interest free to be added to the debt of the farmer is considered to be a solution, then the minister obviously has not looked into the matter.
Last night the minister did a good deal of talking. I do not know why he was belligerent. He will not win many votes for a long time. His handling of this situation certainly would not win him any votes this year in western Canada if there were an election. If the minister really is serious in bringing about a solution to this problem he should sit down with the Prime Minister and decide who will handle this problem. There should be one person appointed who would decide how to solve this problem. It is not a new problem. We learned about it in August last year.

Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act We heard about it in September, October, November, December, January, and now we are in the month of February. It will probably be another three months before the situation comes finally to a head, and if the grain is not dry it will be lost to the farmers and to the economy of the nation.
I have a great deal of respect for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I am also of the opinion that he has far too much responsibility for any minister, even one with his capabilities. He has at least three times the responsibility any minister should assume because it is impossible to do the job well. However, I am sure that when the minister discusses this problem with those who are involved with transportation and transportation facilities in western Canada he will come to the conclusion that it is necessary to have a transport controller in western Canada in order to solve it.
The Minister without Portfolio was wined and dined by the Grains Council, the people who are involved in one aspect of this problem, while he should have been turning his mind to the whole problem. I asked a western farmer about the Grains Council, its membership and what happens when a person brings grain to a country elevator which does not want it. The elevator agent is told he must move it, that there is a necessity that he do it, but I am sure they are not expediting the situation. Mention is made of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways, but I am sure they will not expedite a solution to the problem in western Canada. I am told that it is not as profitable to haul grain as it is to haul almost any other commodity. So the transportation facilities will be used for any purpose other than hauling grain. This will be the last resort when they cannot do anything else.
A controller would allocate the shipping points and see that a certain number of box cars are kept fluid for the transportation of grain at all times. He would decide to what points they would be delivered. In this manner the inequity could be cleared up. There is quite an inequity in respect of the shipping quotas. The controller obviously would work toward rectifying this situation.
Each and every member of this house, if he is really interested in the national good rather than in playing party politics, will be interested in solving the grain crisis in western Canada in the most satisfactory way. I suggest that the minister, instead of lecturing members about things which he does not

If he would look at the problem and see how it has been solved in prior years he would find that the solution is fairly obvious and is one which this government should take.
I think it is a credit to the controllers who have been appointed in years when we have had difficulty that they have been able to solve the problem quietly and efficiently. They have been very pleased when they have terminated their duties to report wholehearted co-operation by the wheat pools, the grain companies, the transportation facilities, the harbour personnel and all other persons connected with the grain industry. They obtained this kind of co-operation. Never since I have been here have they made a report to parliament which indicated they did not receive this kind of co-operation. I suggest that the government does not have the same kind of co-operation. This $600 will only make the farmers $600 poorer. I have been told that 10 cents a bushel for drying grain will not accomplish very much for most of the farmers who have 90 per cent or 100 per cent of their grain in a damp condition.
I hope the Liberal members of this house, on the passing of this legislation, will not thump their desks and say that this is the end of the problem in respect of the grain crisis in western Canada, because I think it is only a start. I was interested to note that the Minister of National Revenue indicated that very little advantage has been taken of the removal of the tariff on grain drying equipment and the provision that certain types of grain storage facilities may be imported without additional cost. These actions really have not done anything to solve the problem. The problem will only be solved when there is equality of opportunity to move damp grain into market position and when we have the full co-operation of and direction over the transportation facilities so that no ships will be standing idle waiting for grain which has been contracted for and then not delivered.
The problem will not be solved until every area in western Canada has a three-bushel quota which will allow the farmers to make arrangements for drying facilities on a cash basis. I suggest that the minister really has not done anything about the problem in western Canada. The introduction of silly pieces of legislation such as this as a solution to a crisis is a pretty ineffective way to solve the problem. I hope the Minister of Industry,

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word or two more about this matter before this legislation passes this afternoon. I regret that the minister in charge is not here. Let me quote briefly from an article which appeared today in the Vancouver Province under the heading "Pepin Hopes But Hedges". Those words do not give a great deal of confidence to the agricultural industry in western Canada. The article states:
The grain crisis in western Canada could be over in a matter of weeks, perhaps in a month, Trade Minister Pepin said Tuesday in Vancouver.
A grain crisis could well develop after the month of March. It was estimated that there were 200 million bushels of damp and tough grain harvested in Alberta alone. It is also estimated that up to this time 15 million bushels of that grain have been shipped or loaded into elevators. It might well be estimated that 85 million bushels have been fed to cattle during the winter or will be fed to cattle before spring. That leaves some 100 million bushels of damp and tough grain in the province of Alberta to be dried between now and spring.
If we assume there are 100 days of cold weather left during which the grain will be preserved, and there will not be that many, we are still left with one million bushels of grain to be dried per day between now and spring. I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman,

to the minister that this crisis will remain with us much longer than another month unless greater action is taken by the government to dry the grain and to assist the farmers to dry more grain on their farms.
As I suggested last night, there are seven ways the government might have acted and might still act to improve the situation in respect of damp grain. Let me suggest one more. Before doing so let me read from an article in the Vancouver Province. It states:
After conferring all day with senior port, transportation and Wheat Board officials, Pepin's smiling optimism at a press conference was mixed with a cautious spreading of blame for the shipping snarls of recent weeks.

This is what I said earlier in the debate on this subject. Damp grain should not have been moved to the coast in greater quantities than could be handled by the grain drying equipment there. Apparently someone thought he might be the saviour of the grain industry by one stroke of the pen. The article then continues:
Both the railways, said the minister, are taking extraordinary steps to make up for delays, but he added that he could not say until noon today, when they are due to report to him, just what further shipping commitments they are prepared to accept.

That is right; the railroads always like to have a little more butter on their bread and a little more cream with their milk. Every year that grain shipments have been large the revenues of the railroads have gone up, and every year that grain shipments

have gone down to a minimum the revenues of the railroad have also gone down. There is no way in which the railroads can say that they can operate on the prairies without hauling grain. The railroads know they are the only ones that can haul grain and so they haul anything else in its place because they know that the grain will wait for them. Grain movement is a national concern and so is the movement of damp grain. The railroads have a monopoly in this field and are morally obligated to share the national concern and to do their utmost to assist the economy of every region of Canada, not only with regard to the wheat problem on the prairies but other problems in other regions of Canada.

May I suggest an alternative method by which the treasury would bear some of these costs. The Wheat Board will be faced with additional costs amounting to millions of dollars because of the difficulty of dealing with tough and damp grain. It will be paying out extra money in demurrage charges on ships and box cars. It will be paying out tens of thousands of dollars in respect of carloads of grain charged as dead freight because grain is light in weight and cars cannot be loaded to the limit. The administration of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act has been marked with tremendous success over the years and the rate of default under the act has been very low. If the hon. member's amendment were adopted and the date changed to March from December, serious inconvenience would be felt by many in an ordinary year.
